caption:
Los Angeles Unified has blocked Google's AI Overviews on school devices.
Google had said schools that turn off its AI would lose Search too.
The district says Google did not help with the block, and it could switch search engines overnight.

Should schools be allowed to use Google without the AI?

site_article.headline: Los Angeles Unified blocks Google's AI Overviews on school devices
site_article.dek: The district found a way to turn off the AI summaries after Google said schools that disable its AI would also lose Search.
site_article.summary: Los Angeles Unified School District has blocked Google's AI Overviews on school-issued devices and says Google played no role in the change. Google had said K-12 schools that do not opt in to its AI products would lose access to Google Search as well.
site_article.seo_title: LAUSD blocks Google AI Overviews on student devices
site_article.seo_description: Los Angeles Unified turned off Google's AI Overviews for students after Google tied school Search access to AI. What the district did and what comes next.
site_article.answer_summary: Los Angeles Unified has disabled Google's AI Overviews for students on district devices, without Google's help, while it reviews whether to keep Google Search at all.
site_article.hero_alt: A hand holds a smartphone showing Google's AI Mode search screen.

paragraphs.text: The Los Angeles Unified School District has blocked Google's AI Overviews, the AI-generated summaries that can appear above regular search results, for students on school-issued devices. District officials confirmed on November 18, 2026 that the feature had been disabled, according to NBC Los Angeles, and Los Angeles Magazine reported on November 27 that the block is now in place.

The district said in a statement that although it keeps an open dialogue with Google, the company did not play a role in the recent changes, Los Angeles Magazine reported. LAUSD has shared few details about how the block works.

The move follows an announcement from Google in early November. The company said its AI products for K-12 student accounts, including the Gemini app, would be turned off by default until school administrators explicitly turn them on. Because Google Search includes AI features by default, schools that keep AI off would lose Search as well, LAist reported.

Chris Phillips, Google's vice president for education, told The New York Times that search and AI are deeply integrated, and that students at schools that ban AI would see a message saying Search is not available, according to both LAist and Los Angeles Magazine. Schools that opt in can use a Guided Learning mode meant to help students work through problems without skipping to the answer.

Google said it is giving schools more choices over AI access, not fewer, NBC Los Angeles reported. According to The New York Times, as cited by NBC, the company declined to offer a version of Search without AI chatbot features.

In September, LAUSD put a moratorium on student use of generative AI on district devices. At the start of the school year, Google helped the district turn off AI Mode, the chatbot-style search, for students signed in with district accounts. Even then, some searches could still show AI summaries, and the district had asked Google for a way to switch them off, LAist reported in early November.

A district spokesperson told NBC Los Angeles that disabling AI Overviews is part of LAUSD's ongoing effort to manage student access to new technology and keep their online experience age-appropriate and safe. The district said it continues to evaluate whether Google Search and other digital tools support student learning.

LAUSD Chief Information Officer Jack Kelanic told a board committee that the district is not bound to Google's products and could change its default search engine overnight, according to Los Angeles Magazine. NBC Los Angeles, citing The New York Times, reported that districts weighing alternatives are looking at DuckDuckGo and Microsoft's Bing, which both offer ways to turn off AI answers.

New York City schools Chancellor Kamar H. Samuels said the city would explore other search options if Google does not reconsider, and Chicago Public Schools said it would look for other solutions if it cannot reach an agreement with Google. Hundreds of Google employees also signed a petition asking the company to let schools turn off AI features, and former Federal Trade Commission chair Lina Khan accused Google of using its search monopoly to coerce schools, Los Angeles Magazine reported.

The Los Angeles block weakens Google's main argument that AI and Search cannot be separated for schools. If one of the largest districts in the country can remove AI Overviews on its own, other districts that want Search without AI have a working example, and Google's opt-in rule looks more like a policy choice than a technical limit.

The next signal is whether Google changes its K-12 policy before the default-off settings take effect, or whether New York City, Chicago or Los Angeles formally switches students to another search engine.
